metadata.description: The official Ryu plugin marketplace — declarative, UI-less tools.

plugins.name: action-summary
plugins.tagline: Make agent actions easy to understand
plugins.description: Explains streamed thinking blocks and tool calls in one plain-language line per action, using a configurable small side model.

plugins.name: activity
plugins.tagline: Everything happening on this node, newest first
plugins.description: The unified activity feed and agent observability workspace: inspect local audits, correlated traces, quality, and security evidence alongside monitor alerts, finished tasks, runs, approvals, meetings, and notes.

plugins.name: advisor
plugins.tagline: A stronger second model reviews your answers
plugins.description: Consult a stronger reviewer model for a second opinion — as an auto-review turn hook (toggle / `/advisor`) and as the model-callable `advisor.consult` tool, a declarative HTTP tool routed through Core's `/api/advisor/consult` bridge.

plugins.name: agent-comms
plugins.tagline: Your agents can message each other
plugins.description: Lets the agents on this node talk to each other. Any agent can look up who else is here, leave one of them a message, and inspect the pair's bounded message history. A message is delivered at the start of the recipient's next turn, so delegation stays asynchronous and scoped to the calling agent. Works with every agent Ryu can run — the flagship agent, Claude Code, Codex, and any custom agent you have added — because it ships as ordinary tools rather than one agent's private feature.

plugins.name: agent-status
plugins.tagline: See which agents are working, stuck, or done
plugins.description: Splits your agent runs across three sidebar sections — Working, Needs input and Done — each row showing the project it belongs to.

plugins.name: agentation
plugins.tagline: Visual feedback for coding agents
plugins.description: Visual feedback for coding agents. Agentation connects UI annotations from a running web app to an MCP server so agents can read, acknowledge, resolve, dismiss, and reply to feedback without copy-paste.

plugins.name: agentbrowser
plugins.tagline: A second real browser for the browser.control layer
plugins.description: Browser automation via the `agent-browser` CLI's MCP server (https://agent-browser.dev). Provides the swappable `browser.control` layer, recording tools, and the documented localhost live stream, so selecting it re-points the stable `browser.*` tools at agent-browser without changing what agents call. Launched from the audited `agent-browser@0.34.0` package; needs Node on PATH.

plugins.name: agents-md-tail
plugins.tagline: Keep project instructions fresh at the end of every turn
plugins.description: Experimental context hook that repeats the active AGENTS.md instructions at the end of the latest message on each model turn, without editing the system prompt or chat history.

plugins.name: ambient-elevator
plugins.tagline: One shared elevator track for active agent runs
plugins.description: Plays one low-volume elevator track while any Ryu agent is actively working, then stops when the last working run ends or needs input.

plugins.name: anydoc
plugins.tagline: Fast local document extraction and API service
plugins.description: Document extraction through Firecrawl's MIT-licensed AnyDoc Rust library. It converts Word, PowerPoint, Excel, OpenDocument, RTF, EPUB, CSV, and text-based PDF files into GitHub-Flavored Markdown through the swappable `document.parse` capability. The local backend is fast and has no model or native-tool download, but it does not OCR scanned pages or fetch URLs. The same out-of-process backend also exposes an API-key-authenticated `/v1/extract` service for direct deployments.

plugins.name: app-studio
plugins.tagline: Drag and drop your own Ryu apps
plugins.description: Build your own Ryu apps with a drag-and-drop visual editor and chat edits, choose the permissions they may ask for, preview them, and install them into Ryu.

plugins.name: approvals
plugins.tagline: Nothing happens until you say yes
plugins.description: Approval inbox: a human-in-the-loop queue where agent-proposed actions, edits, and fixes wait for your accept or reject before they take effect.

plugins.name: auto-continue
plugins.tagline: Never type "continue" again
plugins.description: After each turn while armed, a local sub-agent scans the reply and the workspace for work that is genuinely unfinished and that another turn could complete; if it finds any, it injects a follow-up turn automatically, so a task never stalls waiting for you to type "continue". '/auto-continue off' stops it.

plugins.name: auto-translate
plugins.tagline: Read every reply in your own language
plugins.description: Translates assistant replies that are not in your language, Telegram-style: the original reply stays in the chat and the translation appears beside it. Target language, a do-not-translate list, and the side model are settings.

plugins.name: autopilot
plugins.tagline: Find the wedge before the copy
plugins.description: A positioning-first launch companion. Choose one job, define the market position and narrow ICP, then derive outreach and copy from the same strategy before running bounded Ryu work.

plugins.name: backstage
plugins.tagline: Make thumbnails with your own creative workspace and Ryu AI
plugins.description: A local-first YouTube thumbnail studio that keeps its editor while using Ryu for governed model and image generation.

plugins.name: bitwarden
plugins.tagline: Pull credentials from Bitwarden, not plaintext
plugins.description: Pull API keys from Bitwarden Secrets Manager on demand instead of storing them in plaintext — one machine-account bootstrap token (BWS_ACCESS_TOKEN) replaces N provider keys, and rotating a credential is one change in the Bitwarden web app. Declarative `command` tools that shell out to the locally-installed `bws` CLI (BYO binary, no API key in the manifest).

plugins.name: blueprint
plugins.tagline: Read the plan as a graph, mark it up, and send back a verdict the agent can act on
plugins.description: Review an agent's plan before it touches a file. The agent publishes its plan over MCP; Blueprint parses the markdown into addressable blocks and renders it next to a dependency graph derived from the steps' own `depends_on` edges — so the two questions a wall of markdown cannot answer become visible at a glance: what actually has to happen first, and which step is the one everything else is waiting on. A plan reads as a sequence because prose is a sequence; the work almost never is. You annotate what you object to, anchored to the block or step it belongs to — a comment, a redline carrying the replacement text you want, a question, or a blocker — and then approve or request changes. The verdict is not a mood: it is a document. Requesting changes serializes every annotation into deterministic text the agent reads back through `blueprint.plan_status`, each finding naming the step or block it attaches to and, for a redline, the exact substitution proposed, so a revision answers what was actually written rather than what a summary of it sounded like. Re-publishing under the same plan id appends a revision instead of creating a new plan, and block ids are content-stable across revisions, so the second draft arrives as a diff against the first — the paragraphs you already read are still the paragraphs you already read.

plugins.name: bookmarks
plugins.tagline: Remember why you saved it
plugins.description: A self-organizing bookmark library with HTML/browser imports, notes, inferred collections, and semantic search through Ryu Spaces.

plugins.name: bot-flows
plugins.tagline: Build chat bots from preconfigured flows
plugins.description: Build conversational bots from preconfigured flows for support, lead capture, surveys, and intake, then share or embed them.

plugins.name: brave
plugins.tagline: Search an index nobody else syndicates
plugins.description: Independent web search via the Brave Search API (https://brave.com/search/api/), exposed as one declarative HTTP tool. Provides the swappable `web.search` layer, so selecting it in the layer picker re-points the stable `web.search` tool at Brave's own crawled index without changing what agents call. Brave is search-only: it deliberately declares neither `web.extract` nor `web.crawl`. Requires a BYOK Brave Search API key.

plugins.name: browser
plugins.tagline: Real-Chromium browser control for agents
plugins.description: A real-Chromium browser (Electron) exposed as the grant-gated `browser.control` capability. Local nodes can share one embedded session with the user; managed cloud nodes give each Bot a hidden tab lane with its own persistent Chromium profile, so each agent signs in to sites separately and never sees another agent's cookies, logins, browsing history, site permissions, or downloads. Core routes the desktop Browser panel and agent tools through its authenticated ext-proxy.

plugins.name: browser-use
plugins.tagline: Preview of Browser Use's local browser for Ryu
plugins.description: Preview of Browser Use's open-source local browser as a provider for Ryu's swappable browser.control layer, over its official MCP server (`browser-use --mcp`). Not usable as the Browser layer yet: Ryu starts a fresh browser-use process for every tool call, and browser-use keeps its browser inside that process, so a tab opened by one call is gone by the next. It is hidden from the store while that is the case. The browseruse.* tools stay callable directly, but only a task that finishes within one call, such as retry_with_browser_use_agent, works that way. Launched from the pinned browser-use 0.13.11 package with uvx, with anonymous telemetry and cloud sync off; needs uv on PATH.

plugins.name: bytebot
plugins.tagline: Swap computer control onto a Bytebot desktop
plugins.description: Drives a Bytebot desktop (https://github.com/bytebot-ai/bytebot) through `bytebotd`, its local HTTP daemon, as the SECOND provider of the swappable `computer.control` layer — the first thing that makes that layer actually swappable rather than merely marked selectable. READ THIS BEFORE SELECTING IT: bytebotd drives the desktop IT runs on, which in the shipped Bytebot product is a containerized Linux desktop, NOT the machine running Ryu. Selecting it re-points `computer.capture` / `computer.click` / `computer.type` / `computer.key` / `computer.scroll` away from your own screen (`ghost`, the declared default) and onto that desktop — the same remote-target relationship `browser.control` already has between the local Chromium sidecar and a hosted browser. It serves FIVE of the six canonical verbs: `computer.focus_app` is deliberately NOT bound, because bytebotd's `application` action takes a closed seven-value enum (firefox, 1password, thunderbird, vscode, terminal, desktop, directory) while the canonical verb takes a free-form app name, so any other name would be a schema-legal call that 400s. The app switch is still reachable natively as `bytebot.application`, whose own schema carries that enum so an illegal call cannot be composed. Requires no API key — bytebotd ships with no authentication at all, which is also why this plugin only ever addresses it over loopback. SECURITY, read before enabling: bytebotd ships with NO authentication — no auth middleware, permissive CORS — and this plugin reaches it at the fixed loopback port 9990. Its egress grant is `tool:http-egress:127.0.0.1`, which is HOST-scoped, not port-scoped: approving it grants reach to any service on loopback, not just bytebotd. Only enable this on a machine where you accept that an unauthenticated desktop-control daemon is running and reachable. TARGET: bytebotd drives the desktop IT runs on — in the shipped Bytebot product that is a containerized Linux desktop, NOT the machine running Ryu — so selecting this instead of `ghost` does not give you another way to drive your own computer.

plugins.name: calendar
plugins.tagline: Every scheduled run on one calendar
plugins.description: The scheduled-runs calendar: every agent and workflow scheduled job projected onto Month, Week, Day, and Agenda views — past runs from history, upcoming runs from cron/interval — with a New automation dialog that schedules an agent.

plugins.name: canvas
plugins.tagline: Wire up media, sourced images, and agents
plugins.description: A node board for generative media: wire up image, video, chat, text-to-speech, speech-to-text, upload, and note nodes, search attributed Openverse or node-configured Unsplash images, then run the graph through Ryu's media and agent bridges. Each board persists as a Space document, so it stays editable, shareable, and searchable.

plugins.name: chat-broadcast

Enablement, the first-turn rename, frequency, and the model to use are all settings.

plugins.name: checks

plugins.description: A node-local agentic verification workspace for exploring live targets, generating UI/API plans, running evidence-backed checks, and keeping failure bundles, collections, schedules, and coverage in one place.

plugins.name: clips

Actions go to one target app in the background, through its accessibility tree and screenshots, without moving your cursor. Launched from the pinned, unofficial `codex-computer-use-mcp@0.5.2` stdio bridge. Requires macOS, Node.js 22+, and the ChatGPT app with Computer Use set up; Ryu does not install ChatGPT. Unofficial: a ChatGPT update can break it.

plugins.description: Connect Ryu to Composio's hosted For You MCP server with OAuth. The connection exposes Composio's connected-app tools without requiring a Composio API key; Ryu still applies its own tool allowlists and approval policy.

plugins.name: content
plugins.tagline: Shape ideas into a repeatable publishing system
plugins.description: An unlisted placeholder for a planned local-first content planning app. It ships no interface, runtime, or contributions yet, so it is hidden from the store.

plugins.name: convert
plugins.tagline: Convert files privately on your device
plugins.description: A local-only conversion studio for image output and editing, PDF organization and page rendering, text and structured data, readable DOCX input, ZIP manifest inspection and batch bundles, and Mediabunny browser media conversion. It covers resize, crop, rotate, watermark, split, extract, page numbers, compression, PDF-to-image pages, and MP4/MOV/MKV/WebM/WAV/MP3/Ogg/FLAC/AAC/M4A output without an upload service, Docker dependency, or required sidecar; engine-dependent formats stay input-only.

plugins.name: crm
plugins.tagline: Your pipeline, your schema, your machine
plugins.description: A CRM that starts as a data model rather than a fixed set of screens. Harbor ships the five objects every pipeline needs — companies, people, deals, notes, tasks — and then gets out of the way: add your own objects, give any of them typed fields (currency, status, rating, multi-select, or a relation to another object), and every view, filter, board, and report picks them up without a migration or a settings trip. Records are validated value bags, so a `stage` that used to be free text can become a status field with colours and the old rows keep working. Relations are materialised as real edges in both directions, which is why a company page can show its people, its open deals, and every note anyone wrote against any of them without you modelling the reverse side. Each record carries one unified timeline — notes, calls, meetings, tasks, and the field and stage changes the store writes itself — so "what happened with this account" is one read, not four. CSV import is a first-class flow, not an afterthought: drop a file, see inferred columns with sampled values, map each to an existing field or make a new one, pick a dedupe key, then read a dry run that tells you exactly how many rows would be created, updated, and skipped before anything is written. Duplicates get found and merged field by field, with activities, list memberships, and relation edges reparented onto the survivor. Everything lives in one SQLite database the node owns, indexed with FTS5 for search, and the whole app runs as a sidecar process reached over loopback — no cloud tenant, no seat count, and no third party holding your pipeline.

plugins.name: csharp-lsp
plugins.tagline: C# code intelligence via csharp-ls
plugins.description: C# language server (csharp-ls) for the ryu agent: definitions, references, hover, symbols, implementations, call hierarchies and diagnostics after every edit. You install csharp-ls; the plugin ships config.

plugins.tagline: DeepSeek's own search engine, built for models
plugins.description: Web search and page fetch via the DeepSeek Search / Fetch API (https://api-docs.deepseek.com/guides/search), powered by DeepSeek's in-house search engine and exposed as two declarative HTTP tools. plugins.name: desktop
plugins.tagline: A live, interactive desktop for the node — watch and drive it
plugins.description: An interactive Linux virtual desktop for Ryu nodes. The app sidecar owns stable per-Bot screens on the shared node device and exposes them through Core's authenticated WebSocket proxy with mouse and keyboard input. Files and installed applications remain shared.

plugins.name: dictation
plugins.tagline: Speak anywhere, type anywhere
plugins.description: System-wide dictation and agent-ask hosted by the Island companion: speak anywhere to type a raw or locally cleaned transcript, or ask an agent and paste the answer into the focused app. Requires the Island companion, which is not available in this release, so it is hidden from the store until Island ships.

plugins.name: docling
plugins.tagline: Layout-aware parsing, tables that survive chunking
plugins.description: Document parsing via IBM's MIT-licensed Docling — the highest-fidelity `document.parse` backend. Where a text extractor hands a model a stream of characters, Docling runs real layout analysis: a page-segmentation model finds the reading order, a table-structure model rebuilds merged cells and spanning headers, and the result is exported as markdown whose headings, lists and tables mirror the document's actual structure. That is what makes a multi-column paper or a financial statement survive chunking instead of interleaving into nonsense. The cost is weight: the first parse downloads its models (hundreds of MB) and can take minutes, and every parse after that is CPU-bound inference rather than a string copy. Everything runs locally — Docling explicitly supports air-gapped operation once the models are cached — and no document ever leaves the node. Parses run as jobs: submit returns 202 + a job_id, the caller polls.

plugins.name: docs
plugins.tagline: The Ryu docs, as MCP tools
plugins.description: Read-only MCP access to the Ryu documentation on docs.ryuhq.com — search the docs and pull any page into context as Markdown, without leaving your agent. Backed by the same content /llms.txt serves, exposed as tools by the hosted docs MCP server at https://docs.ryuhq.com/mcp. Ships pre-installed and enabled.

plugins.name: double-check
plugins.tagline: A second model reviews every answer
plugins.description: Sends every answer to a second model for review before you act on it, so mistakes get caught by a fresh set of eyes. Off until you flip the Double-check toggle in the composer; the reviewer model is configurable in settings.

plugins.name: drafts
plugins.tagline: Every unsent message, kept and queued until it can go
plugins.description: A durable outbox for messages you have not sent yet. Anything you type into a composer and walk away from is kept as a draft instead of being lost with the tab, and every draft lives in one node-wide store rather than inside the chat it happened to be typed in — so it survives closing the conversation, restarting the app, and moving to another project. A draft can also be armed: give it a condition and it sends itself when the condition holds. The two conditions that exist are the two that actually block work — 'fewer than N agents are running' (so a queued prompt starts the moment a slot frees instead of piling onto a machine already at capacity) and 'this agent's usage window has room again' (so a prompt written against a capped subscription goes out when the cap lifts rather than failing on send). Both are evaluated against readings the app takes from this node, and a draft whose condition never becomes true simply stays a draft — nothing is sent on a guess.

plugins.name: drawesome
plugins.tagline: Sketch ideas and attach them to chat
plugins.description: A focused sketch surface for Ryu with a compact pen, highlighter, and eraser toolbar, plus chat dialogs for sketching or annotating visual references.

plugins.name: dynamic-workflows
plugins.description: Run bounded delegate fan-outs and durable workflow scripts that orchestrate sub-agents in code.

plugins.name: effort-escalator
plugins.tagline: Spend more reasoning only when work is stuck
plugins.description: Detects stalled work with a cheap background judge and moves the next turn up a configured reasoning-effort or model ladder, per agent or globally.

plugins.name: ego-browser
plugins.tagline: Swap browser control onto Ego lite Spaces
plugins.description: Ego lite (https://github.com/citrolabs/ego-lite) as an optional provider for Ryu's swappable browser.control layer. Immutable operation tools launch the installed ego-browser CLI in a conversation-scoped Ego Space while small adapters preserve the stable browser.* verbs. Tabs, snapshot and screenshot carry read-only effect metadata; navigation, click, type, scroll and the legacy mixed dispatcher are conservatively mutating. Caller input cannot change an operation tool into another action. Requires the Ego lite macOS app and ego-browser on PATH; Ryu does not install Ego lite or copy browser login state.

plugins.name: exa
plugins.tagline: Neural web search for agents
plugins.description: Neural and keyword web search via the Exa API (https://exa.ai), exposed as two declarative HTTP tools: search and find-similar. Requires a BYOK Exa API key.

plugins.name: expanded-composer
plugins.tagline: Write prompts with more room
plugins.description: Expand the current chat composer in place while keeping the same draft, attachments, and send controls.

plugins.name: expect
plugins.tagline: Test agent code in a real browser
plugins.description: Browser-based QA for agent code. Expect reads the current changes, creates a test plan, and runs it in a real browser with Playwright to catch regressions in behavior, performance, security, and design.

plugins.name: expenses
plugins.tagline: A clear view of where the month went
plugins.description: A local-first expense ledger for Ryu: record spending through an agent or the companion, then see totals, categories, and recent entries in one visual view. The node owns the records; no bank connection or exchange-rate conversion is included.

plugins.name: family
plugins.tagline: Birthdays, lists, and gift ideas in one place
plugins.description: A shared family hub for Ryu: important dates with reminders, shared lists and chores, wishlists, and gift ideas that stay hidden from the person they are for. The node your family uses keeps the records; nothing is bought on your behalf.

plugins.name: feedback-board
plugins.tagline: Listen in public. Build with Ryu.
plugins.description: A public feedback board and private Ryu product workspace: collect requests, votes, and comments, turn demand into a roadmap, and use configurable Ryu workflows to prepare or build what users ask for.

plugins.name: finetune
plugins.tagline: Train a model on your own data, on your own GPU
plugins.description: A local SFT and DPO training studio: launch LoRA/QLoRA jobs on this node's GPU or a remote Ryu Cloud GPU node, compare preferred and rejected answers, merge the trained adapter to GGUF, and register the result as a swappable local model.

plugins.name: firecrawl
plugins.tagline: Search and scrape the web for agents
plugins.description: Web search and page scraping via the Firecrawl v2 API (https://firecrawl.dev), exposed as two declarative HTTP tools. Provides the swappable `web.search` and `web.extract` layers, so selecting it in the layer picker re-points the stable `web.search` / `web.extract` tools at Firecrawl without changing what agents call. Requires a BYOK Firecrawl API key.

plugins.name: firewall
plugins.tagline: Turn on the Gateway's prompt-injection and PII screen
plugins.description: An on/off switch over the Gateway's built-in firewall, which screens model traffic for prompt injection and PII. Enabling this plugin forces `firewall.enabled` on at the next Gateway restart; the pattern set and policy mode stay owned by the Gateway config (GET/PUT /v1/config), not by this plugin.

plugins.name: honcho
plugins.tagline: A standing synthesis of the user, not a list of facts
plugins.description: Give the swappable `memory` layer a provider that MODELS the user instead of only storing rows, via Honcho (https://honcho.dev) — the Plastic Labs identity layer Hermes uses for exactly this. Honcho watches the messages you hand it and derives a per-peer REPRESENTATION; its Dialectic endpoint (`POST /v3/workspaces/{workspace_id}/peers/{peer_id}/chat`) then answers a natural-language question about that peer with its own synthesis. That is what the canonical `memory.context` verb has always promised and no shipped provider served, so this is the first plugin to make the kernel's `context` bridge (`memory.provider-context`) do anything at all. Honcho here serves TWO verbs: `memory.context` (the Dialectic synthesis) and `memory.search` (`POST .../peers/{peer_id}/search`, documented as "Search a Peer's messages" — conversation text, not the conclusions Honcho derives from it, which matters because the `prefetch` bridge is on by default and will start injecting message excerpts each turn). It also binds the two WRITE verbs, `memory.sync` and `memory.store`, through an adapter. Honcho's only documented write is `POST /v3/workspaces/{workspace_id}/sessions/{session_id}/messages`, whose `messages[]` items each require a `peer_id` — a NESTED position the declarative `arg_template` cannot reach, because a template substitutes only from CALLER arguments and never sees a resolved `pref:`. That is why both verbs went unbound and why `memory.mirror-builtin` (default ON) was inert. An adapter receives those `pref:` values already resolved, so the per-install peer lands inside `messages[]` without hardcoding one bucket for every install. The session and both peers are caller-named and created on first write, so nothing has to be set up by hand; Ryu's own replies are written as a SEPARATE peer, since attributing an assistant turn to your peer would poison the representation Honcho derives about you. `memory.forget` stays unbound: Honcho documents no message-delete endpoint, which no adapter can invent. The built-in store's own `memorystore.save` tool and this node's per-turn memory write are kernel and untouched. Every call is scoped to one workspace and one peer, both set per install in the settings tab — a hardcoded pair would put every install in one shared bucket. Requires a BYOK Honcho API key.

plugins.name: markitdown

plugins.description: Document parsing via Microsoft's MIT-licensed MarkItDown library — the default `document.parse` backend, and the one that works on a machine where the user installed nothing on purpose. `pip install 'markitdown[all]'` is a pure-Python install of a few tens of megabytes: no ONNX runtime, no layout-detection model download, no GPU, and no `brew`/`apt` packages to chase. plugins.name: mem0
plugins.tagline: Recall and record in an existing Mem0 project inside Ryu
plugins.description: Read and write a hosted Mem0 memory project (https://mem0.ai) through the Mem0 Platform REST API, exposed as three declarative HTTP tools. The SECOND provider of the swappable `memory` layer — the built-in store stays the default and keeps running alongside it — so selecting Mem0 re-points the stable `memory.search` / `memory.store` / `memory.sync` / `memory.forget` tools at your Mem0 project without changing what agents call, and turns on the kernel bridges that fold Mem0 into every turn's recall and echo this node's writes out to it. The one canonical verb Mem0 does NOT serve is `memory.context`: Mem0 publishes no standing-summary endpoint, and forcing the verb onto its get-all would dump raw facts at system rank under a label promising a synthesis. The two WRITE verbs both post to `POST /v3/memories/add/`, which is ASYNCHRONOUS — it answers `{message, status: "PENDING", event_id}` and never a fact id — so `memory.store` returns an accepted-for-processing envelope, not the id of the fact it created, and nothing may chain `memory.forget` onto its result. That is fine for the way both verbs are used: the kernel `mirror` and `sync` bridges are fire-and-forget and never read the response. The two verbs differ in ONE documented field: `store` sends `infer: false` because the caller has already decided the fact and Mem0 should keep the text as-is, while `sync` hands over a raw turn with Mem0's default inference on and lets Mem0 mine it. Note the entity id lives in two different places in Mem0's own API — nested inside `filters` for search, top-level for add — and both are pinned from the same `mem0.user-id` preference. Requires a BYOK Mem0 API key.

plugins.name: mineru
plugins.tagline: Scientific and scanned PDFs, formulas to LaTeX
plugins.description: Document parsing via MinerU (opendatalab) — the highest-fidelity `document.parse` backend, and the heaviest. Built for scientific and scanned PDFs: it runs layout detection to reconstruct true reading order across multi-column pages, converts formulas to LaTeX, converts tables to HTML, and OCRs scanned pages, so a physics paper comes back as markdown a model can actually follow instead of two columns interleaved line by line. The cost is real: MinerU wants Python 3.10-3.13, 16 GB of RAM (32 GB recommended), about 20 GB of disk for its model set, and a 4 GB-VRAM GPU for the pipeline backend (8 GB for the VLM backends) to be quick — a CPU-only host works through the `pipeline` backend but parses take minutes. Models download on first use. MinerU ships as a CLI, so each parse is a supervised subprocess with a hard wall-clock kill: a timed-out or cancelled parse takes its whole process group with it rather than leaving a multi-gigabyte orphan. Parses run as jobs: submit returns 202 + a job_id, the caller polls.

plugins.name: news
plugins.tagline: Every outlet covering the same story, collapsed into one
plugins.description: Your own newsroom, running on your node. Wire pulls RSS, Atom and JSON Feed in on a schedule — parsed natively, with conditional GET, per-source backoff, and a source marked `failing` after three consecutive misses rather than quietly going silent — then does the work an aggregator does for you and never shows its working. Duplicates die twice: URLs are canonicalized (redirects followed, `utm_*` and friends stripped, query pairs sorted) and content is fingerprinted with a banded 64-bit SimHash over word shingles, which is what catches one wire story running under six different headlines on six different sites. What survives is clustered across outlets by shingle similarity, entity overlap and title overlap, so the unit you read is a story with *n* sources attached and a visible spread of framings, not the same paragraph six times. A watch is a real boolean query — `AND` / `OR` / `NOT`, phrases, `title:` and `source:` scoping — parsed to an AST and evaluated against tokenized text, and it refuses to save on a parse error with the column, because a watch that silently matches nothing is worse than one that will not save. Breaking is defined, not guessed: a topic's hourly volume against a baseline built from the same hour of day over the trailing week, carrying its z-score and the articles that caused it. Ranking is recency half-life × source count × topic match × unread, every factor displayable. A model is involved in exactly two places — two sentences per cluster in the brief, and one neutral headline for a story eight outlets titled eight ways — and the raw cluster stays inspectable underneath both. Nothing leaves the node but the fetches, and those go to the sources you added.

plugins.name: pxpipe

This plugin owns the process lifecycle (spawn, health, restart) and mounts pxpipe's dashboard behind Core auth. It is a TRANSPARENT proxy and holds no credential of its own: it forwards whatever key its caller sends, so point a custom provider at http://127.0.0.1:47821 with your own API key (see README). plugins.name: reasoning
plugins.tagline: Prove the answer follows the policy — or find the counterexample
plugins.description: Check an answer against a written policy with a solver instead of a second opinion. Point it at a document — an HR handbook, a refund policy, an underwriting rule sheet — and it drafts a formal model of it: typed variables and rules you can read and edit in plain language. From then on, a question and an answer are translated into logic and decided by a decision procedure built from scratch here (finite-domain enumeration over booleans and enums, Fourier–Motzkin elimination over linear rational arithmetic, branch-and-bound for integers). The result is not a score: `valid` means the policy PROVES the answer, `invalid` means it CONTRADICTS it and comes with a concrete counterexample, `satisfiable` means the policy simply does not settle it, and `impossible` means the policy contradicts itself — the case a naive checker silently reports as approval. Every finding names the minimal set of rules that decided it, the facts the answer quietly assumed, and what would have had to be different, all read back out of the solver rather than written by a model. Exact rational arithmetic throughout, so a rule about 0.1 + 0.2 does not fail on floating point. Model calls happen only at the two language edges; the verdict is reproducible offline from the formulas.

plugins.name: rlm
plugins.tagline: Ask a question of more text than a model can hold
plugins.description: Answer questions about a corpus far larger than any model's context window — without putting it in a prompt. The usual options all degrade: truncate and you lose the answer, embed-and-retrieve and you get fragments without their argument, buy a bigger window and attention over the middle of it thins out anyway. This app does the other thing. Your documents are held here as a variable. A root model plans over an outline of them — chunk ids, sources, line spans, headings — and reaches the text only through operators that summarise before returning: `grep` to locate, `map` to run a cheap model over the chunks that matter in parallel and fold the answers back, `recurse` to give a sub-question its own plan over a subset. The root model never sees the corpus, so its context stays roughly the same size whether you point it at 40 KB or 40 MB, and the answer does not get worse as the input gets bigger. Every answer carries `path:line` citations read back out of the chunks it rests on, and every run keeps a full trace — each operator, each sub-call, what it cost — that you can open and replay. Depth, step, call and wall-clock budgets are hard: a run that hits one says so and returns what it had, rather than quietly shortening the answer. Agents get the same engine as tools, and `grep` and `peek` need no model at all, so a workflow can branch on a deterministic search of a 40 MB corpus. Capability callers may query an existing context or submit bounded inline documents that are persisted as a context and analyzed in the same recursive run.

"What should I study next" is a topological answer — the weakest skill whose prerequisites you have already mastered — not a guess, and "0.62 mastery, three more correct at this difficulty reaches 0.9" is a projection you can check by hand. Multiple-choice, cloze, numeric-with-tolerance and exact answers are graded by comparison with no model in the loop at all; only free-response answers are marked by a model, and those always show the rubric they were graded against. Given an exam date it projects, from your observed rate over the last ten sessions, whether the syllabus will be covered in time, and says `unknown` rather than extrapolating off two data points. entries.name: blueprint
entries.tagline: Read the plan as a graph, mark it up, and send back a verdict the agent can act on
entries.description: Review an agent's plan before it touches a file. The agent publishes its plan over MCP; Blueprint parses the markdown into addressable blocks and renders it next to a dependency graph derived from the steps' own `depends_on` edges — so the two questions a wall of markdown cannot answer become visible at a glance: what actually has to happen first, and which step is the one everything else is waiting on. A plan reads as a sequence because prose is a sequence; the work almost never is. You annotate what you object to, anchored to the block or step it belongs to — a comment, a redline carrying the replacement text you want, a question, or a blocker — and then approve or request changes. The verdict is not a mood: it is a document. Requesting changes serializes every annotation into deterministic text the agent reads back through `blueprint.plan_status`, each finding naming the step or block it attaches to and, for a redline, the exact substitution proposed, so a revision answers what was actually written rather than what a summary of it sounded like. Re-publishing under the same plan id appends a revision instead of creating a new plan, and block ids are content-stable across revisions, so the second draft arrives as a diff against the first — the paragraphs you already read are still the paragraphs you already read.

entries.name: bytebot
entries.tagline: Swap computer control onto a Bytebot desktop
entries.description: Drives a Bytebot desktop (https://github.com/bytebot-ai/bytebot) through `bytebotd`, its local HTTP daemon, as the SECOND provider of the swappable `computer.control` layer — the first thing that makes that layer actually swappable rather than merely marked selectable. READ THIS BEFORE SELECTING IT: bytebotd drives the desktop IT runs on, which in the shipped Bytebot product is a containerized Linux desktop, NOT the machine running Ryu. Selecting it re-points `computer.capture` / `computer.click` / `computer.type` / `computer.key` / `computer.scroll` away from your own screen (`ghost`, the declared default) and onto that desktop — the same remote-target relationship `browser.control` already has between the local Chromium sidecar and a hosted browser. It serves FIVE of the six canonical verbs: `computer.focus_app` is deliberately NOT bound, because bytebotd's `application` action takes a closed seven-value enum (firefox, 1password, thunderbird, vscode, terminal, desktop, directory) while the canonical verb takes a free-form app name, so any other name would be a schema-legal call that 400s. The app switch is still reachable natively as `bytebot.application`, whose own schema carries that enum so an illegal call cannot be composed. Requires no API key — bytebotd ships with no authentication at all, which is also why this plugin only ever addresses it over loopback. SECURITY, read before enabling: bytebotd ships with NO authentication — no auth middleware, permissive CORS — and this plugin reaches it at the fixed loopback port 9990. Its egress grant is `tool:http-egress:127.0.0.1`, which is HOST-scoped, not port-scoped: approving it grants reach to any service on loopback, not just bytebotd. Only enable this on a machine where you accept that an unauthenticated desktop-control daemon is running and reachable. TARGET: bytebotd drives the desktop IT runs on — in the shipped Bytebot product that is a containerized Linux desktop, NOT the machine running Ryu — so selecting this instead of `ghost` does not give you another way to drive your own computer.

entries.name: crm
entries.tagline: Your pipeline, your schema, your machine
entries.description: A CRM that starts as a data model rather than a fixed set of screens. Harbor ships the five objects every pipeline needs — companies, people, deals, notes, tasks — and then gets out of the way: add your own objects, give any of them typed fields (currency, status, rating, multi-select, or a relation to another object), and every view, filter, board, and report picks them up without a migration or a settings trip. Records are validated value bags, so a `stage` that used to be free text can become a status field with colours and the old rows keep working. Relations are materialised as real edges in both directions, which is why a company page can show its people, its open deals, and every note anyone wrote against any of them without you modelling the reverse side. Each record carries one unified timeline — notes, calls, meetings, tasks, and the field and stage changes the store writes itself — so "what happened with this account" is one read, not four. CSV import is a first-class flow, not an afterthought: drop a file, see inferred columns with sampled values, map each to an existing field or make a new one, pick a dedupe key, then read a dry run that tells you exactly how many rows would be created, updated, and skipped before anything is written. Duplicates get found and merged field by field, with activities, list memberships, and relation edges reparented onto the survivor. Everything lives in one SQLite database the node owns, indexed with FTS5 for search, and the whole app runs as a sidecar process reached over loopback — no cloud tenant, no seat count, and no third party holding your pipeline.

entries.name: docling
entries.tagline: Layout-aware parsing, tables that survive chunking
entries.description: Document parsing via IBM's MIT-licensed Docling — the highest-fidelity `document.parse` backend. Where a text extractor hands a model a stream of characters, Docling runs real layout analysis: a page-segmentation model finds the reading order, a table-structure model rebuilds merged cells and spanning headers, and the result is exported as markdown whose headings, lists and tables mirror the document's actual structure. That is what makes a multi-column paper or a financial statement survive chunking instead of interleaving into nonsense. The cost is weight: the first parse downloads its models (hundreds of MB) and can take minutes, and every parse after that is CPU-bound inference rather than a string copy. Everything runs locally — Docling explicitly supports air-gapped operation once the models are cached — and no document ever leaves the node. Parses run as jobs: submit returns 202 + a job_id, the caller polls.

entries.name: honcho
entries.tagline: A standing synthesis of the user, not a list of facts
entries.description: Give the swappable `memory` layer a provider that MODELS the user instead of only storing rows, via Honcho (https://honcho.dev) — the Plastic Labs identity layer Hermes uses for exactly this. Honcho watches the messages you hand it and derives a per-peer REPRESENTATION; its Dialectic endpoint (`POST /v3/workspaces/{workspace_id}/peers/{peer_id}/chat`) then answers a natural-language question about that peer with its own synthesis. That is what the canonical `memory.context` verb has always promised and no shipped provider served, so this is the first plugin to make the kernel's `context` bridge (`memory.provider-context`) do anything at all. Honcho here serves TWO verbs: `memory.context` (the Dialectic synthesis) and `memory.search` (`POST .../peers/{peer_id}/search`, documented as "Search a Peer's messages" — conversation text, not the conclusions Honcho derives from it, which matters because the `prefetch` bridge is on by default and will start injecting message excerpts each turn). It also binds the two WRITE verbs, `memory.sync` and `memory.store`, through an adapter. Honcho's only documented write is `POST /v3/workspaces/{workspace_id}/sessions/{session_id}/messages`, whose `messages[]` items each require a `peer_id` — a NESTED position the declarative `arg_template` cannot reach, because a template substitutes only from CALLER arguments and never sees a resolved `pref:`. That is why both verbs went unbound and why `memory.mirror-builtin` (default ON) was inert. An adapter receives those `pref:` values already resolved, so the per-install peer lands inside `messages[]` without hardcoding one bucket for every install. The session and both peers are caller-named and created on first write, so nothing has to be set up by hand; Ryu's own replies are written as a SEPARATE peer, since attributing an assistant turn to your peer would poison the representation Honcho derives about you. `memory.forget` stays unbound: Honcho documents no message-delete endpoint, which no adapter can invent. The built-in store's own `memorystore.save` tool and this node's per-turn memory write are kernel and untouched. Every call is scoped to one workspace and one peer, both set per install in the settings tab — a hardcoded pair would put every install in one shared bucket. Requires a BYOK Honcho API key.

entries.name: mem0
entries.tagline: Recall and record in an existing Mem0 project inside Ryu
entries.description: Read and write a hosted Mem0 memory project (https://mem0.ai) through the Mem0 Platform REST API, exposed as three declarative HTTP tools. The SECOND provider of the swappable `memory` layer — the built-in store stays the default and keeps running alongside it — so selecting Mem0 re-points the stable `memory.search` / `memory.store` / `memory.sync` / `memory.forget` tools at your Mem0 project without changing what agents call, and turns on the kernel bridges that fold Mem0 into every turn's recall and echo this node's writes out to it. The one canonical verb Mem0 does NOT serve is `memory.context`: Mem0 publishes no standing-summary endpoint, and forcing the verb onto its get-all would dump raw facts at system rank under a label promising a synthesis. The two WRITE verbs both post to `POST /v3/memories/add/`, which is ASYNCHRONOUS — it answers `{message, status: "PENDING", event_id}` and never a fact id — so `memory.store` returns an accepted-for-processing envelope, not the id of the fact it created, and nothing may chain `memory.forget` onto its result. That is fine for the way both verbs are used: the kernel `mirror` and `sync` bridges are fire-and-forget and never read the response. The two verbs differ in ONE documented field: `store` sends `infer: false` because the caller has already decided the fact and Mem0 should keep the text as-is, while `sync` hands over a raw turn with Mem0's default inference on and lets Mem0 mine it. Note the entity id lives in two different places in Mem0's own API — nested inside `filters` for search, top-level for add — and both are pinned from the same `mem0.user-id` preference. entries.name: news

Duplicates die twice: URLs are canonicalized (redirects followed, `utm_*` and friends stripped, query pairs sorted) and content is fingerprinted with a banded 64-bit SimHash over word shingles, which is what catches one wire story running under six different headlines on six different sites. What survives is clustered across outlets by shingle similarity, entity overlap and title overlap, so the unit you read is a story with *n* sources attached and a visible spread of framings, not the same paragraph six times. A watch is a real boolean query — `AND` / `OR` / `NOT`, phrases, `title:` and `source:` scoping — parsed to an AST and evaluated against tokenized text, and it refuses to save on a parse error with the column, because a watch that silently matches nothing is worse than one that will not save. Breaking is defined, not guessed: a topic's hourly volume against a baseline built from the same hour of day over the trailing week, carrying its z-score and the articles that caused it. Ranking is recency half-life × source count × topic match × unread, every factor displayable. A model is involved in exactly two places — two sentences per cluster in the brief, and one neutral headline for a story eight outlets titled eight ways — and the raw cluster stays inspectable underneath both. Nothing leaves the node but the fetches, and those go to the sources you added.

entries.name: reasoning
entries.tagline: Prove the answer follows the policy — or find the counterexample
entries.description: Check an answer against a written policy with a solver instead of a second opinion. Point it at a document — an HR handbook, a refund policy, an underwriting rule sheet — and it drafts a formal model of it: typed variables and rules you can read and edit in plain language. From then on, a question and an answer are translated into logic and decided by a decision procedure built from scratch here (finite-domain enumeration over booleans and enums, Fourier–Motzkin elimination over linear rational arithmetic, branch-and-bound for integers). The result is not a score: `valid` means the policy PROVES the answer, `invalid` means it CONTRADICTS it and comes with a concrete counterexample, `satisfiable` means the policy simply does not settle it, and `impossible` means the policy contradicts itself — the case a naive checker silently reports as approval. Every finding names the minimal set of rules that decided it, the facts the answer quietly assumed, and what would have had to be different, all read back out of the solver rather than written by a model. Exact rational arithmetic throughout, so a rule about 0.1 + 0.2 does not fail on floating point. Model calls happen only at the two language edges; the verdict is reproducible offline from the formulas.

entries.name: rlm
entries.tagline: Ask a question of more text than a model can hold
entries.description: Answer questions about a corpus far larger than any model's context window — without putting it in a prompt. The usual options all degrade: truncate and you lose the answer, embed-and-retrieve and you get fragments without their argument, buy a bigger window and attention over the middle of it thins out anyway. This app does the other thing. Your documents are held here as a variable. A root model plans over an outline of them — chunk ids, sources, line spans, headings — and reaches the text only through operators that summarise before returning: `grep` to locate, `map` to run a cheap model over the chunks that matter in parallel and fold the answers back, `recurse` to give a sub-question its own plan over a subset. The root model never sees the corpus, so its context stays roughly the same size whether you point it at 40 KB or 40 MB, and the answer does not get worse as the input gets bigger. Every answer carries `path:line` citations read back out of the chunks it rests on, and every run keeps a full trace — each operator, each sub-call, what it cost — that you can open and replay. Depth, step, call and wall-clock budgets are hard: a run that hits one says so and returns what it had, rather than quietly shortening the answer. Agents get the same engine as tools, and `grep` and `peek` need no model at all, so a workflow can branch on a deterministic search of a 40 MB corpus. Capability callers may query an existing context or submit bounded inline documents that are persisted as a context and analyzed in the same recursive run.

entries.name: spidercloud
entries.tagline: Hosted site crawling, no local binary
entries.description: Hosted multi-page web crawling via the Spider Cloud API (https://spider.cloud), exposed as one declarative HTTP tool. Provides the swappable `web.crawl` layer as a SECOND provider alongside the local `spider` CLI, so selecting it re-points the stable `web.crawl` tool at a hosted crawler that needs no local binary. The crawl is synchronous — `run_in_background` defaults to false and one request returns every fetched page's content, so there is no job id to poll. The canonical `depth` argument is deliberately DROPPED: Spider Cloud documents `depth: 0` as "no limit will be applied", the exact inverse of the canonical contract's "0 = the start page only". Requires a BYOK Spider Cloud API key.

entries.name: steel

Not usable as the Browser layer yet: Ryu starts a fresh Steel server process for every tool call, and the session handle that browser.navigate gets back exists only inside the process that created it, so the next call cannot use it. It is hidden from the store while that is the case. Steel's stateless tools that take a URL directly, such as steel_scrape, stay available under steel.*. Needs a Steel API key stored as the STEEL_API_KEY vault secret and Node on PATH.

entries.name: tuition
entries.tagline: Drill the weakest thing you are ready for, graded by arithmetic
entries.description: A tutor for one learner — you. Point it at your own syllabus, chapter or notes and it builds a mastery model you can read: every skill carries a Bayesian Knowledge Tracing posterior, its prerequisite edges, and a spaced-repetition schedule computed in whole days so a review due tomorrow does not move because you studied at 23:58. "What should I study next" is a topological answer — the weakest skill whose prerequisites you have already mastered — not a guess, and "0.62 mastery, three more correct at this difficulty reaches 0.9" is a projection you can check by hand. Multiple-choice, cloze, numeric-with-tolerance and exact answers are graded by comparison with no model in the loop at all; only free-response answers are marked by a model, and those always show the rubric they were graded against. Given an exam date it projects, from your observed rate over the last ten sessions, whether the syllabus will be covered in time, and says `unknown` rather than extrapolating off two data points. A model is used at exactly two edges — proposing skills from a document, and writing practice items and rubric marks — and both are reviewed by a person before they count.

entries.name: unstructured
entries.tagline: Sixty formats, element-typed output
entries.description: Document parsing via the Apache-2.0 Unstructured library — the broadest-coverage `document.parse` backend, reading roughly sixty formats (PDF, the whole Office family including the legacy binary .doc/.ppt/.xls, email, EPUB, HTML, spreadsheets, and OCR over scanned images). Its distinguishing output is element-level: every fragment comes back typed (Title, NarrativeText, ListItem, Table, CodeSnippet, PageBreak), so the sidecar can emit markdown that preserves document structure instead of a flat text dump — headings stay headings and tables stay tables through chunking. The cost is install weight: `unstructured[all-docs]` is a 1-2 GB Python install, and the native tools it shells out to (poppler, tesseract, libreoffice, pandoc) are NOT pip-installable and must be present on the host. The sidecar detects each missing tool and reports it by name through the job's `error`/`missing_dependencies` fields rather than failing as an empty document. Parses run as jobs: submit returns 202 + a job_id, the caller polls.
